caveats: **No documented business driver.** The priority for this plugin is asserted from a capability-gap reading, not evidenced by any tracked demand (see "How it works"); there is no capability-map requirement, named customer, SOC 2 control or CVE behind it.

**Configuration, not evaluation — and on Windows `audit_policy`, not the effective audit state.** Linux and macOS report what the files state, not what PAM or sudo would decide: `pwquality.conf.d` and `faillock` drop-ins are not read, `sudoers` include directives are listed and not followed, `audit.rules` counts are of the file and not the live kernel rules, and a `pwpolicy` expression is reported verbatim (only `minimum_length` is derived from it). The sharpest case is Windows `audit_policy`: `secedit /export` returns the nine **legacy** `[Event Audit]` categories, and where Advanced Audit Policy subcategories are in force — the Windows 10/11 default, and the norm under GPO — those are not what the host actually audits. A category reading `none` means the legacy category is unset, **not** that the host is not auditing; the committed rig capture is exactly that shape (a default Windows 11 Pro, all nine `none`). `auditpol /get /category:*` is the effective state and is not read — that would be a second argv leaf with its own sink-manifest row.

**The Windows leg is measured on real hardware — a standalone host.** It is rung 2 by design; a rig session captured a real `secedit /export` as LocalSystem, confirming `SeSecurityPrivilege` suffices with the privilege in its default Disabled state (fixture, sample and the `RIG PROBE` banner in `local_security_policy_win.cpp` all reflect this). That host was **not domain-joined**: on a domain-joined member the export is the local security database *after* GPO application, and domain-account password policy is not reported at all.

**Privileged files read as `unreadable` for an unprivileged agent.** `/etc/sudoers` (`0440`), `/etc/sudoers.d/*` and Linux `/etc/audit/audit.rules` (`0640`) need root or a read-override capability; without it the action reports `PERMISSION_DENIED`, never an empty list. macOS `audit_control` is absent by default and reads `absent`.

**Global scope only, unmanaged captures, and no cross-OS normalisation.** macOS `pwpolicy` is queried for the global account policies, not per-user policies, and the Windows export covers the local security policy area only (no domain policy resultant set, no `auditpol` subcategories beyond `[Event Audit]`). The macOS captures are from an **unmanaged** Mac, so whether an MDM configuration-profile passcode payload surfaces in `pwpolicy -getaccountpolicies` is unverified — on a managed device `lockout_policy|policies|none` must not be read as "no lockout enforced". Separately, keys are each OS's own vocabulary and are deliberately **not** normalised: the same fact is `MinimumPasswordLength` on Windows, `PASS_MIN_LEN` (or pwquality's `minlen`) on Linux and `minimum_length` on macOS, so a fleet-wide "weaker than our baseline" query has to branch per OS. The `source` field names the origin on every row; no normalised column is offered.

definitions.description: Reports the local audit policy. Linux reads /etc/audit/audit.rules and reports rule, watch-rule and syscall-rule counts, lines it does not model, and the -e state (enabled, disabled, immutable or unset), from the rule file only, not the live kernel rules; macOS reads /etc/security/audit_control, which is absent by default on current macOS (reported `absent`, not a failure); Windows reports every [Event Audit] category from one `secedit /export` as none, success, failure or success_failure. Those are the LEGACY audit categories: where Advanced Audit Policy subcategories are in force -- the Windows 10/11 default and the norm under GPO -- they are not the effective audit state, so a category reading none means the legacy category is unset, NOT that the host is not auditing. `auditpol /get /category:*` is the effective state and is not read. audit.rules is 0640 root, so an unprivileged Linux agent reports `unreadable` and PERMISSION_DENIED.

Reports the local account lockout policy as one row per setting. Linux reads the lockout keys of login.defs, faillock.conf and the faillock/tally lines of the auth and account stacks in /etc/pam.d; macOS reads the authentication policies from `pwpolicy -getaccountpolicies` (no authentication policy reports `policies|none`, the default); Windows reads LockoutBadCount, ResetLockoutCount and LockoutDuration from one `secedit /export`. It reports configuration, not live lockout counters. A source the OS reports missing reads `absent`; one that could not be read reads `unreadable` with a reason and downgrades the result, never an empty success. Keys are each OS's own vocabulary and are deliberately NOT normalised across platforms, so a fleet-wide comparison must branch per OS.

Reports the local password policy as one row per setting: which setting, its value and where it was read. Linux reads login.defs, pwquality.conf and the password stacks in /etc/pam.d (pwquality, pwhistory, cracklib and unix module lines); macOS reads the global account policies from `pwpolicy -getaccountpolicies`; Windows reads MinimumPasswordAge, MaximumPasswordAge, MinimumPasswordLength, PasswordComplexity, PasswordHistorySize and ClearTextPassword from one `secedit /export`. It reports what the configuration states, not the live PAM or LSA decision. A source the OS reports missing reads `absent`; one that could not be read reads `unreadable` with a reason and downgrades the result to CONSTRAINED or PERMISSION_DENIED, never an empty success. Keys are each OS's own vocabulary and are deliberately NOT normalised across platforms (Windows MinimumPasswordLength, Linux PASS_MIN_LEN or pwquality minlen, macOS minimum_length all state a minimum length), so a fleet-wide comparison must branch per OS.

Reports the parsed content of /etc/sudoers and every file in /etc/sudoers.d, one row per Defaults line, alias, include directive or user spec. Include directives are listed, not followed; a line the parser does not recognise is kind `unmodelled` with the raw line, never dropped; a file sudo would skip by name is kind `ignored`. Reading /etc/sudoers needs root or the file's group (0440), so an unprivileged agent reports kind `unreadable` and PERMISSION_DENIED, never an empty list. Linux and macOS only; Windows has no sudoers.

description: Reports local password, lockout and audit policy posture and sudoers content
how_it_works:
Four read-only actions (`local_security_policy_plugin.cpp`) report a host's local security policy: `password_policy`, `lockout_policy`, `audit_policy` and `sudoers`. Each writes pipe-delimited rows, the first field being the action name, then `<key>|<value>|<source>` (`sudoers` rows carry `<file>|<kind>|<subject>|<runas>|<nopasswd>|<commands>`). No action takes parameters, so no request text reaches a path or an argv. Nothing is ever written, configured or imported.

- **Linux (rung 1, bounded file reads):** `/etc/login.defs`, `/etc/security/pwquality.conf`, `/etc/security/faillock.conf`, the password and auth/account stacks under `/etc/pam.d` (`pam_pwquality`, `pam_pwhistory`, `pam_cracklib`, `pam_unix`, `pam_faillock`, `pam_tally2`, `pam_tally`), `/etc/audit/audit.rules` (rule, watch-rule, syscall-rule, unmodelled-line and control-line counts and the `-e` state -- `rules` is the RULE count, equal to `watch_rules + syscall_rules + unmodelled_lines`, while `control_lines` counts the `-D`/`-b`/`-f`/`-e` style directives that configure auditd rather than add a rule, so a stock file of nothing but control directives correctly reports `rules|0`), and `/etc/sudoers` plus `/etc/sudoers.d`.
- **macOS:** `password_policy` and `lockout_policy` come from `pwpolicy -getaccountpolicies`, a **rung-2** argv leaf (one spawn per action, sink `local_security_policy/do_password_policy#1`), because no public OpenDirectory global-policy API exists; the plist is parsed with `CFPropertyListCreateWithData`, never a hand-rolled scanner. `audit_policy` reads `/etc/security/audit_control` (absent by default on current macOS) and `sudoers` reads `/etc/sudoers` and `/etc/sudoers.d`.
- **Windows (rung 2, not rung 1):** `password_policy`, `lockout_policy` and `audit_policy` share one `secedit.exe /export /areas SECURITYPOLICY` argv leaf (sink `local_security_policy/do_export#1`), parsed from its UTF-16LE INI (`[System Access]` and `[Event Audit]`). The roadmap first drafted this leg as `NetUserModalsGet`/`LsaQueryInformationPolicy` at rung 1; the tree has no LSA policy-query precedent, `NetUserModalsGet` was passed over, and `docs/agent-privilege-model.md` names `secedit /export` the authoritative source on a running box, so the leg is declared rung 2 and the descriptor, the capability matrix and this page all say so. `sudoers` has no Windows leg.

**Scratch directory and stale sweep (Windows).** `secedit` writes the export itself, so each dispatch creates its own directory `local_security_policy-<32 hex>` under `agent.data_dir` (random 128-bit name, created with `CREATE_NEW`, owner-only DACL), holds it open, checks it is the agent's own, and removes it on every path the process survives. With `agent.data_dir` unset the action reports `constrained|data_dir_unset`: there is no fallback location. A crash or service stop between the export and the delete would orphan a copy of the machine's policy, so every dispatch first sweeps `local_security_policy-<32 hex>` directories older than one hour under `agent.data_dir`, ownership-verified (a same-named directory owned by another SID is skipped; a non-flat one is left intact). The sweep outcome is logged only, never a row or a token.

Every source reads as exactly one of three things: a **value**, **`absent`** (the OS definitively reports the file, key or directory is not there) or **`unreadable`** (the read failed). A failed read never reads as absent, and absence is not a failure: an `absent` row adds no reason token and does not lower the status. A refused read reports `PERMISSION_DENIED`; any other failure reports `CONSTRAINED` with one `<source>:<cause>` token. A value the tables cannot interpret is named `unmodelled`, never dropped.

**Why this plugin exists (stated plainly, not inflated).** Zero documented driver anywhere: not even a tangential mention across capability-map, enterprise-parity, the SOC 2 doc or `docs/roadmap.md` (the capability-map plugin-inventory row is added by this change as a listing, not a driver). The SOC 2 doc's Workstream B (Identity/Access/Admin Security) covers RBAC/SSO/MFA for **Yuzu's own** admin accounts, with zero overlap with a managed endpoint's local security policy. This is pure capability-gap reasoning, not evidenced demand.

outputs_note: Pipe-delimited rows via `write_output()`. The first field is the fixed literal action name (`password_policy`, `lockout_policy`, `audit_policy` or `sudoers`), then `<key>`, `<value>` and `<source>` (for `sudoers`: `<file>`, `<kind>`, `<subject>`, `<runas>`, `<nopasswd>`, `<commands>`). Every field passes through the shared untrusted-output escaper. A key present with no value reads `present`. A source that is missing or unreadable is one `source_state` row (`absent`, or `unreadable:<token>`). Windows keys the export does not carry read `absent`. macOS reports `policies|none` when no matching policy is set, which is the default. Row output is capped at 4096 rows (`row_cap`). When a non-OK outcome produced no rows at all — today only a failed `pwpolicy` run (spawn error, deadline, truncated output, non-zero exit, no plist or an unparseable one) — the action writes one `<action>|status|<state>|<reason>` row rather than an empty result: the third field is `constrained` or `permission_denied` and the fourth carries the reason token, not a source. File-backed and `pwpolicy` failures are data-level outcomes and the action returns 0; a Windows failure and an internal exception return 1 with the single row `constrained|<token>` — that two-field row is the Windows leg's generic failure tag and reads `constrained` even when the typed status is `PERMISSION_DENIED` (the status field and the token, e.g. `secedit:access_denied`, carry the distinction); `sudoers` on Windows returns 1 with the row `sudoers|-|unsupported|-|-|-|windows_has_no_sudoers` and status `UNAVAILABLE`.

privileges.grant: `secedit /export` needs an elevated token. The agent already holds `SeSecurityPrivilege` (`scripts/install-agent-user.ps1`, granted for the Security event log); measured on the-rig as LocalSystem: `SeSecurityPrivilege` suffices with the privilege in its default **Disabled** state, nothing else was granted or needed (the `RIG PROBE` banner in `local_security_policy_win.cpp`, `docs/samples/windows.txt`)
privileges.if_refused: `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED` reading the export reports `PERMISSION_DENIED` with `secedit:access_denied`; a non-zero `secedit` exit reports `CONSTRAINED` with `secedit:exit_<n>`; the action returns 1 with the row `constrained|<token>`
privileges.measured: Yes: a real `secedit` export from the-rig is committed as `tests/unit/fixtures/wave8/local_security_policy/windows/secedit_export.inf` (1,274 bytes, UTF-16LE — a trim of the full 12,828-byte export down to the `[Unicode]`/`[System Access]`/`[Event Audit]` sections the plugin actually reads; see the fixture's own `.provenance.txt`)

privileges.grant: None for `pwpolicy -getaccountpolicies`; `/etc/sudoers` is `root:wheel` `0440`, so reading it needs root or group wheel
privileges.if_refused: `EACCES` on `/etc/sudoers` reports the row kind `unreadable` with `permission_denied` and the action reports `PERMISSION_DENIED`/`PARTIAL`; a failed `pwpolicy` run reports `CONSTRAINED` with `pwpolicy:<cause>`
privileges.measured: 2026-09-21, bare-metal, this Mac (`braga`), unprivileged (euid 501): real capture (`docs/samples/macos.txt`); no root-privileged run has been captured
privileges.runs_as: agent daemon, root today (LaunchDaemon carries no `UserName` key, `docs/agent-privilege-model.md` TL;DR)

privileges.grant: None for the world-readable config; `/etc/audit/audit.rules` (`0640`) and `/etc/sudoers` plus `/etc/sudoers.d/*` (`0440`) need root or a read-override capability
privileges.if_refused: `EACCES`/`EPERM` reports the source `unreadable` with `<path>:permission_denied`; the action reports `PERMISSION_DENIED` when nothing else was readable, otherwise `CONSTRAINED`; a missing file (`ENOENT`) reports `absent` with no token
privileges.measured: Fixtures are real captures from a default and a hardened container (`tests/unit/fixtures/wave8/local_security_policy/linux/`); the live sample under `docs/samples/linux.txt` is a container run of the built `.so` as root

result_status.when: Every source was read or definitively `absent`. An absent source adds no token, so a default macOS host with no `audit_control` reports `OK`.
Linux and macOS file reads: at least one source failed for a reason other than a refusal (or a refusal while something else was readable); the reason lists one `<source>:<cause>` token per failure.
macOS `password_policy` and `lockout_policy`: the `pwpolicy` run or its plist failed.
Windows: the scratch directory or the `secedit` run or export failed; the action returns 1 with the row `constrained|<token>`.
Any leg: an unexpected exception was contained in `execute()`; the action returns 1 with the row `constrained|internal_error`.
A read was refused and nothing else was readable (file legs), or the Windows export could not be read (`ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED`).

where_the_data_goes: **Instruction result.** Rows travel over the agent's mTLS gRPC channel as the command response and land in the ResponseStore, queryable at `/api/responses/{id}`. Each action is a gathered definition (`crossplatform.local_security_policy.<action>`, 300s TTL).
**Not consumed by** daily-sync, TAR, DEX, or metrics.

**Sensitivity.** Password, lockout and audit rows are a compliance baseline of the host (a short minimum length, no lockout, auditing off), which is useful to an attacker choosing a target. `sudoers` rows carry account and group names, run-as targets, `NOPASSWD` flags and command paths, i.e. exactly who may become root. Treat all four like other `Security` data.
**Siblings:** `firewall`, `bitlocker` and `antivirus` (other `Security` posture plugins) and `users` (account and group membership; this plugin reports policy, not accounts).
